newsitem.title: UK: Clarke faces Hague in fight for UK Tory leader.
newsitem.headline: Clarke faces Hague in fight for UK Tory leader.

text.p: The contest to lead Britain's battered Conservative party headed on Tuesday for a third and final ballot after a second vote reduced the field to a straight left-right fight between Kenneth Clarke and William Hague.

Clarke, a former finance minister and outspoken pro-European, won the votes of 64 of the main opposition party's 164 members of parliament against 62 for Hague, an ex-Welsh secretary who is on the party's moderate right wing.
John Redwood, a prominent Eurosceptic former cabinet minister, was eliminated from the contest to succeed ex-prime minister John Major as party leader after polling just 38 votes.
The run-off ballot will take place on Thursday.

Clarke had not been expected to win on Tuesday, but bookmakers William Hill immediately installed Hague as 1-3 favourite on the assumption that he would attract the bulk of Redwood's supporters on the far right of the party.

"I'm well satisfied with the results of the second ballot... I think I now have the momentum and the support to win the third ballot on Thursday," said a beaming Hague, who at 36 would be the youngest Conservative leader in more than 200 years.
But Clarke's backers were confident their man would pick up enough votes from the Redwood camp to carry him to victory.
After all, they noted, Clarke won 15 votes on Tuesday from two other right-wing challengers who dropped out after the first round of voting a week ago.
"I think today is an extremely encouraging result. I'm glad we're we now in the final furlong, but I think we're obviously going to win," Clarke said.

The problem facing the Conservatives is that the contest has only served to highlight the splits over Europe that contributed to their defeat in the May 1 election, when they were crushed by Tony Blair's Labour party after 18 years in power.

Before Thursday's ballot, Clarke bitterly attacked Hague for hardening his line against the European Union's planned single currency in an opportunistic pitch for the votes of Conservative Eurosceptics deeply hostile to further European integration.
"That is not the campaign of a unity candidate. That is the campaign of a candidate who's trying to settle an old issue," Clarke told BBC radio.

He accused Hague of changing his position several times before finally demanding that any MPs who wanted to serve in his "shadow" cabinet -- which will monitor the work of the real cabinet -- must declare their opposition to scrapping the pound.

This would rule out Clarke, who has said it would be folly for Britain to close off the option of joining the single currency, thereby raising the spectre of a parliamentary Conservative party still deeply divided along European lines.
Hague, perhaps realising his task of harrying Blair would be hopeless if he could not unite his MPs, immediately started to build bridges to Clarke's camp after the vote.
If he won, he said, he would set out to unite the party "including all strands of opinion within it".
